title: Widescreen Fights Back
objective: After this level you can explain why movies went wider and bigger in the 1950s as television kept audiences at home.
summary: As TV kept people home, attendance fell by almost half from 1946 to 1956. Hollywood went wide: three-projector Cinerama in 1952, then CinemaScope's squeezed image in 1953.

cards.headline: In 1946, two out of three Americans went to the movies every week.
cards.body: The studios earned record profits. Then a new box arrived in the living room. Hollywood's answer was a picture far bigger than any television could show.

cards.headline: Movies in the home
cards.body: Network television, spreading from the 1940s, gave Hollywood its first real rival for people's free time: moving pictures without leaving home. By 1956 movie attendance was down almost 50 percent from its 1946 peak. So Hollywood turned to color and widescreen, things that set a night at the movies apart from television.

cards.headline: Cinerama: three projectors, one wall
cards.body: First came Cinerama, launched in New York in 1952 with This Is Cinerama. Three synchronized projectors each threw a third of the picture onto a wide, curving screen. It was a popular novelty, but its costs were prohibitive, and it was abandoned in the 1960s.

cards.headline: CinemaScope: squeeze and stretch
cards.body: The winner was simpler. CinemaScope added a special lens to the camera that squeezed a wide picture onto ordinary 35 mm film. In the theater, a projection lens stretched it back out, onto a screen about two and a half times as wide as it was tall. Twentieth Century-Fox launched it with The Robe in 1953, and by the late 1950s most major studio films were made for wide screens.
